- **Retrace your exact footsteps back the way you came**, stepping precisely in your own prints.
- If you cannot see your own prints, stay where you are and call for help.
- **Stay on hard-surfaced, well-used roads and paths.** Mines are placed on shoulders, verges, shortcuts, and in likely stopping places.
- **Warning signs of mined areas:** red-painted stones or red triangles, skull-and-crossbones signs, fencing, dead livestock, abandoned fields adjacent to cultivated ones, and areas villagers avoid without explanation. **Ask locals — they always know.**

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 7: Checkpoints and Armed Personnel
children.text:
- **Approach slowly, hands visible and empty.** At night, put the interior light on in a vehicle and slow down early.
- **Do not make sudden movements. Do not reach into a bag or a pocket without saying what you are doing first.**
- **Carry ID at all times.** Aadhaar, and any residence or permit document required in your area.
- **Answer questions briefly and factually.** Do not argue, do not joke, do not film, do not ask for names or numbers.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 7: Checkpoints and Armed Personnel
children.text:
- **Do not photograph checkpoints, military installations, bridges, or convoys.** This is an offence and will be treated as hostile.
- **Follow the vehicle in front at a distance** and do not overtake a military convoy.
- **If detained,** stay calm, comply, and ask to inform a family member. Note names, times, and the unit if you safely can.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 8: Evacuation and Displacement
children.text:
- **Go early.** Roads close, fuel runs out, and trains fill. Families who wait for certainty get trapped.
- **Follow the official evacuation route** if one is designated; unofficial routes may be mined, shelled, or blocked.
- **Travel in daylight** where possible, and in a group.
- **Take:** ID for every person including children, cash in small notes, water, ORS, dry food, medicines and prescriptions, phone and powerbank, torch, warm clothing, and a written list of contacts.
- **Mark your house** on departure: names, number of people, destination, date.
- **Register at the relief camp** or with the district administration on arrival.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 8: Evacuation and Displacement
children.text: - **Keep the family together and keep children physically attached to an adult.** Family separation is the single largest harm in displacement.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 8: Evacuation and Displacement
children.text: - **Do not carry anything that could be read as a weapon or as partisan material.**

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 9: Water, Food and Health in a Prolonged Conflict
children.text:
- **Water is the first thing to fail.** Fill everything at the first warning. Assume the supply will be contaminated or cut. Boil or chlorinate everything. See the **Water, Food and Sanitation** guide.
- **Food:** stock non-perishable, no-cook items. Ration from day one, not from the day you notice supplies running low.
- **Medicines:** chronic patients — diabetics, cardiac, dialysis, TB, epilepsy, psychiatric — are at the greatest risk in a prolonged conflict, not the wounded. **Get 30 days of medication in advance** and keep the prescription on paper.
- **Sanitation:** a covered bucket with a lid, ash or lime, and a designated disposal point away from water. Disease kills far more civilians in prolonged conflicts than weapons do.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 9: Water, Food and Health in a Prolonged Conflict
children.text:
- **Do not gather in large groups**, including at water points, markets, and relief distributions, for longer than necessary.
- **Keep a battery radio.** All India Radio is the official information channel and it will keep broadcasting.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 10: Nuclear or Radiological Event
children.text:
Extremely unlikely, but the protective actions are simple and worth knowing.
- **If you see an intense flash, do not look at it.** Drop flat, face down, feet towards it, hands over your head and ears, mouth open. Stay down for at least a minute — the blast wave follows the flash.
- **Then get inside, immediately, and get as deep and central as you can.** A basement or the middle of a large concrete building. Distance and mass are the only protection.
- **Stay inside for at least 24 hours, preferably 48.** Fallout radiation decays extremely fast — it drops by roughly 90% in the first 7 hours and 99% in about 2 days. Going outside early is far more dangerous than staying put without food.

children.heading_path: War, Air Raids and Border Conflict (India) > Part 10: Nuclear or Radiological Event
children.text:
- **Remove outer clothing** if you were outside — this removes most contamination — and bag it away from you. **Shower with soap and lukewarm water**, no conditioner (it binds particles to hair). Blow your nose and wipe your eyelids and ears.
- **Seal the room** — close windows and doors, switch off AC and exhaust fans, tape gaps.
- **Drink only bottled or sealed water and food from sealed containers.** Food inside a sealed packet or a fridge is safe.
- **Potassium iodide (KI)** protects only the thyroid, only from radioactive iodine, and only if taken at the right time. **Take it only when authorities instruct you to.** Do not take it speculatively, do not exceed the dose, and do not use iodine antiseptic or iodised salt as a substitute — that is dangerous and useless.
- **Listen to All India Radio for instructions.**

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India)
children.text: India has dense industrial belts sitting immediately next to dense housing: Bhopal, Vapi, Ankleshwar, Manali and Ennore in Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Dahej, Taloja and Chembur in Mumbai, Ludhiana, Kanpur, Panipat, and hundreds of smaller estates. The Bhopal gas disaster of 1984 remains the world's worst industrial accident and the pattern of that night — people running into the gas rather than away from it — is the single most important lesson in this guide.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India)
children.text: **The core rule: gas is heavier than air in almost every case that matters. Go UP and go UPWIND.**

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 1: Recognising a Release
children.text:
- An unusual smell: chlorine (bleach, swimming pool), ammonia (sharp, urine-like), rotten eggs (hydrogen sulphide), garlic or almonds, sweet or fruity solvent smells, or a sharp acid bite in the throat
- **A visible cloud, mist, or haze low to the ground**, often white, yellow-green, or brown
- **A siren from a nearby factory.** Most Indian chemical plants have an on-site emergency siren. Know what yours sounds like.
- People, animals, or birds collapsing, coughing, or fleeing
- Sudden eye watering, throat burning, or coughing across many people at once
- Vegetation suddenly wilting or discolouring

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 1: Recognising a Release
children.text: **Important:** **hydrogen sulphide destroys your sense of smell within seconds.** If a rotten-egg smell disappears suddenly while you are still in the area, that is a lethal sign, not a good one. Get out.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 2: Immediate Actions
children.text:
**Decide first: escape or shelter.**
**ESCAPE if** you can see the cloud, you know where it is, and there is a clear route upwind or uphill that does not pass through it.
**SHELTER if** you cannot tell where the cloud is, it is already around you, or you are downwind with no clear route out.
If escaping:
1. **Move UPWIND — into the wind, so the wind is in your face.** Check the wind direction with dust, smoke, a flag, or a wet finger.
2. **Move UPHILL and go UP inside a building.** Chlorine, ammonia (in cold conditions), LPG, and most industrial vapours collect at ground level and flow into low ground, drains, basements, and pits.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 2: Immediate Actions
children.text:
3. **Move at right angles to the wind, then upwind.** Running straight away downwind keeps you inside the plume.
4. **Cover your nose and mouth with a cloth, wet if possible.** For ammonia and chlorine, a cloth wet with plain water helps considerably.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 2: Immediate Actions
children.text: 5. **Do not run.** Running triples your breathing rate and pulls more gas into your lungs. **Walk fast, breathe shallowly through the cloth.** This is precisely the error that killed thousands in Bhopal.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 2: Immediate Actions
children.text:
6. **Do not go into a basement, an underground parking, or a low-lying area.**
7. **Take children with you — carry them.** They are shorter and therefore deeper in the gas layer.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 2: Immediate Actions
children.text:
8. **Do not use a vehicle if it means driving through the cloud.**
If sheltering in place:
1. **Go to the highest floor**, to a room with the fewest windows and doors, preferably an interior bathroom.
2. **Close all doors and windows.** Switch off all AC, exhaust fans, chimney, and any ventilation that draws outside air in.
3. **Seal the room.** Wet cloth or tape along door gaps, tape over vents and keyholes, plastic sheet over windows.
4. **Keep a wet cloth over your nose and mouth.**
5. **Turn on a radio** for instructions.
6. **Stay put until the all-clear.** Do not go out to check.
7. If you must leave later, cover up completely, cover your face, and go upwind.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**Chlorine** (water treatment plants, swimming pools, bleaching, transported in cylinders)
- Yellow-green gas, smells of bleach, much heavier than air, hugs the ground
- **Go up and upwind.** Never go down.
- Causes burning eyes, throat, coughing, and chest tightness; at high concentration, fluid in the lungs (pulmonary oedema) hours later
- **Anyone exposed needs 24 hours of observation** even if they feel fine

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**Ammonia** (cold storages, ice plants, dairies, fertiliser units — extremely common in India)
- Sharp, unmistakable, intensely irritating
- Lighter than air when warm but forms a dense cold cloud on release, so it can hug the ground initially
- **Water is your friend** — a wet cloth over the face genuinely works because ammonia dissolves readily in water
- Flush eyes and skin with lots of water for at least 20 minutes

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**Hydrogen sulphide** (sewers, septic tanks, tanneries, oil refining, drains)
- Rotten eggs at low concentration, **odourless at lethal concentration**
- This is what kills sanitation workers in Indian septic tanks and manholes every year

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text: - **Never enter a manhole, septic tank, sewer, or unventilated pit to rescue someone who has collapsed.** Multiple deaths in a chain — the rescuer, then the next rescuer — is the standard Indian pattern. Ventilate first, and use a rope and a harness from outside.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**LPG and natural gas** (household, industrial, pipelines)
- LPG is heavier than air and pools at floor level, in drains, and in basements
- **No sparks. No switches. No phones. No flames.** Ventilate, close the valve, evacuate, call **1906**

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**Pesticides and organophosphates** (agricultural India, both accidental and intentional)
- Absorbed through skin, lungs, and gut
- Signs: pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation and sweating, vomiting, muscle twitching, difficulty breathing, confusion
- **Remove contaminated clothing, wash the skin thoroughly with soap and water**, and get to a hospital urgently — atropine is the antidote and PHCs stock it

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
- **Do not induce vomiting.** Take the container or a photograph of the label.
**Acids and alkalis** (industrial, and acid attacks)
- **Flush with large volumes of running water for at least 20-30 minutes, continuously.**

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
- **Do not try to neutralise** — the reaction generates heat and worsens the burn
- Remove contaminated clothing while flushing
- Alkali burns (caustic soda, lime) are deeper and more damaging than acid burns and need longer flushing

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 3: Specific Common Indian Hazards
children.text:
**Radiological sources** (industrial radiography, hospital equipment, orphaned sources in scrapyards)
- If you find an unfamiliar heavy metal container with a trefoil radiation symbol, **do not touch it, do not open it, do not take it to a scrap dealer.** Move away, keep others away, and inform the police and the AERB.
- Time, distance, and shielding are the three protections. Increase all three.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 4: Decontamination
children.text:
For anyone who has been in a chemical cloud or splashed:
1. **Get to fresh air and away from the source first.**
2. **Remove clothing — cut it off rather than pulling it over the head.** Removing outer clothing removes the large majority of contamination.
3. **Bag the clothing** and keep it away from people. Do not shake it out.
4. **Wash with lots of water and soap**, from head down, for at least 15 minutes. Lukewarm, not hot — hot water opens pores and increases absorption.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 4: Decontamination
children.text:
5. **Do not scrub hard** — abrasion drives chemicals into the skin.
6. **Flush eyes for 20 minutes** with clean water, holding the eyelids open, from the inner corner outward so contaminated water does not run into the other eye. **Remove contact lenses.**
7. **For dry powder, brush it off first** before adding water. Some chemicals react violently with water.
8. **Wash hair last**, and do not use conditioner.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 5: Treating the Exposed
children.text:
- **Protect yourself first.** Contaminated casualties will contaminate you. Use gloves, cover your face, and work upwind.
- **Fresh air and rest.** Do not let them walk or exert themselves — exertion increases absorption and worsens lung injury.
- **Sit them upright** if they are breathless.
- **Give oxygen if available.**

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 5: Treating the Exposed
children.text:
- **Do not give anything by mouth** if they are drowsy or vomiting.
- **Watch for delayed lung injury.** Chlorine, phosgene, ammonia, and smoke can all cause fluid in the lungs 6-24 hours after exposure, in someone who initially seemed fine. **Any significant inhalation exposure needs 24 hours of observation.**
- **Keep the chemical name or a photograph of the container** and send it with them to hospital.
- **Poison information:** the **National Poisons Information Centre at AIIMS Delhi (011-26593677 / 26589391)** operates 24 hours.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 6: If You Live Next to an Industrial Estate
children.text:
- **Find out what is stored there.** Under the Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules and the Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, Major Accident Hazard (MAH) units must have an off-site emergency plan and the district must publish it. Ask the district collectorate or the factory inspectorate.
- **Learn the plant siren signal** and what it means.
- **Know the prevailing wind direction** for your area in each season, and identify your upwind escape route in advance.
- **Identify the assembly point** in the off-site emergency plan.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 6: If You Live Next to an Industrial Estate
children.text:
- **Keep N95 masks and a supply of clean water at home.**
- **Participate in mock drills** if your district runs them. They are the only realistic rehearsal you will get.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 6: If You Live Next to an Industrial Estate
children.text: - **Do not build or sleep in the low-lying area between the plant and the housing.** Gas flows downhill.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 7: Confined Spaces — Septic Tanks, Manholes, Wells, Silos
children.text:
This kills more Indians every year than any industrial disaster, and it is entirely preventable.
- **Never enter a septic tank, manhole, sewer, disused well, grain silo, or tanker without testing the atmosphere, forced ventilation, a harness with a rope tended from outside, and a breathing apparatus.**
- **Manual scavenging is illegal in India** under the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013. Employing anyone to enter a sewer or septic tank without protective equipment is a criminal offence.
- **If someone collapses inside: DO NOT GO IN AFTER THEM.** This is how two, three, and four people die instead of one. The gas that dropped them will drop you within seconds.

children.heading_path: Industrial Accidents, Gas Leaks and Chemical Exposure (India) > Part 7: Confined Spaces — Septic Tanks, Manholes, Wells, Silos
children.text:
- **From outside:** shout for help, call 112 and the fire service, ventilate with a blower or by fanning, and if there is a rope on the person, pull them out from outside.
- **The atmosphere may be oxygen-deficient rather than toxic.** You cannot smell missing oxygen. Unconsciousness is instant.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India)
children.text: Heat kills more Indians than any other weather hazard. Heatwaves in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Vidarbha, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Delhi routinely exceed 45 C, with wet-bulb conditions in coastal and eastern India that are physiologically more dangerous still. Cold waves in north India — Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar — kill hundreds of homeless and rural people every winter, and the Himalayan states face genuine hypothermia risk year-round at altitude.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 1: Heat — Understanding the Danger
children.text:
**IMD heatwave criteria:** a heatwave is declared when the maximum temperature reaches at least 40 C in the plains, 37 C on the coast, or 30 C in the hills, **and** is 4.5-6.4 C above normal. A **severe heatwave** is a departure of over 6.4 C, or an absolute maximum of 45 C (47 C for severe).
**Humidity matters more than temperature.** A dry 45 C in Jaisalmer is survivable in shade with water. A humid 38 C in Kolkata or Chennai can be more lethal, because sweat cannot evaporate and the body loses its only cooling mechanism. Watch the "feels like" / heat index, not just the thermometer.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 1: Heat — Understanding the Danger
children.text:
**Highest risk:**
- Outdoor workers — construction, agriculture, delivery riders, street vendors, traffic police
- Infants and children under 5
- Adults over 65
- Pregnant women
- People with heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes, or obesity
- People on diuretics, antihistamines, antipsychotics, or beta-blockers
- People living in tin-roofed or asbestos-roofed houses, and in top-floor rooms
- Anyone without access to shade, water, or a fan during a power cut

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text:
**Heat cramps** — painful muscle spasms, usually in the legs or abdomen, after exertion and sweating.
- Stop, move to shade, rest
- Give ORS or salted water or nimbu-pani with salt

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text:
- Do not resume heavy work for several hours
**Heat exhaustion** — the body is losing the fight but is still compensating.
- **Signs:** heavy sweating, cool and clammy pale skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, fast weak pulse, muscle cramps, thirst, irritability, fainting
- **Treatment:** move to shade or an air-conditioned space, lie down, raise the legs, remove excess clothing, cool the skin with wet cloth and fanning, give ORS or cool water in small frequent sips
- **This is the warning stage. Act now and it does not become heat stroke.**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text:
**Heat stroke — a medical emergency. This kills.**
- **Signs:** body temperature above 40 C; **confusion, agitation, slurred speech, seizures, or unconsciousness**; skin that is hot and often **dry** because sweating has stopped (though in exertional heat stroke the skin may still be wet); rapid breathing; a racing pulse; flushed skin
- **The distinguishing sign is a change in mental state.** A hot person who is confused, aggressive, or drowsy has heat stroke until proven otherwise.
- **Treatment — cool them aggressively and immediately. Cooling is the treatment; nothing else matters as much.**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text:
1. Move to shade at once
  2. **Remove all outer clothing**
  3. **Pour water over them continuously and fan hard.** Evaporative cooling in Indian conditions is highly effective and requires only water and a piece of cardboard.
  4. **Put ice packs, cold water bottles, or wet cloth in the armpits, groin, neck, and behind the knees** — where large blood vessels run near the surface
  5. **If a tub, tank, or drum is available, immerse them in cold water up to the neck** — this is the fastest cooling method and it saves lives. Hold the head above water.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text: 6. **Do not give fluids to an unconscious person.**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text: 7. **Do not give paracetamol or aspirin.** They do not work for heat stroke and aspirin worsens bleeding risk.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 2: The Three Heat Illnesses
children.text:
8. **Do not use alcohol rubs.**
  9. **Get to a hospital**, but cool them first and continue cooling on the way. The first 30 minutes decide the outcome.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
**Water**
- Drink before you are thirsty. Thirst is a late signal in the heat.
- **Check your urine.** Pale straw yellow is fine. Dark yellow or amber means you are already dehydrated. Not passing urine for 8 hours is an emergency sign.
- Water alone is not enough during heavy sweating — you lose salt too. **ORS, nimbu-pani with salt and sugar, chaas/buttermilk, aam panna, coconut water, and sattu** all replace both.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
- **Avoid alcohol, strong tea and coffee in excess, and sugary carbonated drinks** — all worsen dehydration.
- If you have kidney or heart disease and have been told to limit fluids, ask your doctor before increasing intake.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
**Behaviour**
- **Stay indoors between 12 noon and 4 pm.** Reschedule all outdoor work to before 11 am and after 5 pm.
- If you must be outside: rest in shade for 10 minutes every hour, wear a wet cloth or gamcha on your head and neck, and drink continuously.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
- **Never leave a child, an elderly person, or an animal in a parked vehicle.** The interior reaches 60 C+ in minutes even with windows cracked. This kills every summer.
- **Wear loose, light-coloured, cotton clothing.** Cover your head outdoors — a cap, a gamcha, a dupatta, or an umbrella. A wet cloth on the head is genuinely effective.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
**Keeping a house cool without power**
- **Close windows, curtains, and shutters during the day** on the sun-facing side; open everything at night for cross ventilation
- **Wet a bedsheet or a khus/vetiver mat and hang it in the window.** Air passing through evaporates and cools — this is a genuinely effective traditional Indian technique
- **Wet the floor and the terrace** in the evening
- **Cool the roof.** A white lime wash, white paint, or a layer of straw, coconut leaves, or thermocol on a tin or concrete roof drops the indoor temperature by several degrees. This is the single highest-value intervention for tin-roofed homes.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
- **Sleep on the floor or the terrace at night** — hot air rises
- **Wet a cloth and place it on the neck, wrists, and behind the knees**
- **Take cool showers**, or wet the arms and legs frequently
- **Turn off unnecessary electrical appliances** — they add heat

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text:
**Watch other people**
- **Check on elderly neighbours living alone at least twice a day.** Isolated elderly people are the largest heatwave death group and they will not ask for help.
- Watch infants for fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes or fontanelle, no tears when crying, and lethargy. Give ORS and seek help.
- Provide water for street animals and birds.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 3: Surviving a Heatwave
children.text: **Heat Action Plans:** Ahmedabad pioneered India's first city Heat Action Plan and dozens of cities now have them. They include cooling centres, extended hospital hours, water points, and rescheduled work timings. **Find out whether your city has one and where the cooling centres are.**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text:
**IMD cold wave criteria:** minimum temperature at or below 10 C in the plains with a departure of 4.5 C or more from normal, or a minimum at or below 4 C regardless.
**Cold kills in India at temperatures people dismiss as mild.** Most Indian cold deaths occur between 5 and 12 C, in people who are wet, undernourished, exposed, or alcohol-affected. Wet clothing at 10 C is more dangerous than dry clothing at 0 C.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text:
**Hypothermia stages:**
- **Mild:** shivering, cold hands and feet, tiredness, poor coordination, slurred speech
- **Moderate:** violent shivering, confusion, apathy, stumbling, poor judgement ("paradoxical undressing" — removing clothes because they feel hot)
- **Severe:** **shivering stops** — this is the critical danger sign, not an improvement — rigid muscles, slow weak pulse, shallow breathing, unconsciousness

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text:
**Treatment:**
1. **Get them out of the wind and off the ground.** The ground steals heat faster than the air. Put something insulating underneath — cardboard, a mat, dry leaves, a bag.
2. **Remove wet clothing** and replace with dry, or wrap in a dry blanket over the wet clothing if there is nothing dry.
3. **Insulate the whole body including the head and neck.** Most heat is lost from the head and the torso.
4. **Warm the core, not the limbs.** Warm packs or bottles at the chest, armpits, groin, and neck. **Do not rub the arms and legs** — this pushes cold blood back into the core and can stop the heart.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text:
5. **Skin-to-skin contact inside a shared blanket** is highly effective.
6. **Warm sweet drinks only if fully conscious and able to swallow.** Tea with sugar is ideal.
7. **No alcohol.** It feels warming and it accelerates heat loss dangerously. Alcohol is involved in a large share of Indian cold deaths.
8. **Handle very gently.** In severe hypothermia, rough movement can trigger cardiac arrest.
9. **In severe hypothermia, "nobody is dead until they are warm and dead."** Continue CPR and warming — people have recovered fully from apparently absent vital signs.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text:
**Frostbite** (Himalayan states, high passes, Ladakh):
- Signs: numbness, white or waxy skin, hard to the touch
- **Rewarm in water at 37-39 C** — comfortably warm to your elbow, never hot

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text: - **Do not rub with snow, do not use direct heat, do not use a fire or a heater**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text: - **Do not rewarm if there is any chance of refreezing** — walking on a frozen foot is far better than walking on a thawed one that refreezes

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 4: Cold Wave and Hypothermia
children.text: - Do not burst blisters; get medical care

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 5: Surviving a Cold Wave
children.text:
- **Layer clothing.** Several thin layers trap air and work far better than one thick one. The inner layer should not be wet cotton against the skin — cotton loses all insulation when damp.
- **Cover head, ears, neck, hands, and feet.** These lose heat fastest.
- **Stay dry.** Change out of wet clothes immediately.
- **Eat and drink.** The body needs fuel to generate heat. Hot food, hot drinks, and enough calories matter more than people realise.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 5: Surviving a Cold Wave
children.text: - **Do not use a coal angithi, a charcoal sigri, or a kerosene heater in a closed room.** This is the classic Indian winter killer — **carbon monoxide poisoning kills whole families in their sleep** every winter in north India. If you must use one, keep a window open on two sides and never sleep with it burning.

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 5: Surviving a Cold Wave
children.text: - **Do not use an LPG stove or a generator indoors for heat.**

children.heading_path: Heatwave and Cold Wave (India) > Part 5: Surviving a Cold Wave
children.text:
- **Do not drink alcohol to keep warm.**
- **Check on the elderly, the homeless, infants, and people living alone.** Night shelters (rain baseras) are run by municipal corporations in north Indian cities during cold waves; the numbers are published by the district administration.
- **Protect water pipes and livestock** in the hills.
- **Watch for exacerbations of heart and lung disease.** Cold weather increases heart attacks, strokes, and asthma attacks. Keep inhalers and cardiac medicines to hand.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India)
children.text: India has the highest snakebite mortality in the world — roughly 58,000 deaths a year, overwhelmingly in rural areas, overwhelmingly at night, and overwhelmingly among farmers and their families. Almost all of these are preventable, and almost all of them involve delay caused by traditional first aid that does not work.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India)
children.text: **The one thing that saves lives is anti-snake venom (ASV) in a hospital. Everything in the first aid section exists only to get the person there alive and unharmed by well-meaning treatment.**

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 1: The Big Four
children.text:
Indian polyvalent ASV is manufactured against four species, which cause the large majority of deaths:
**1. Spectacled Cobra (Naja naja / nag)**
- Hood with spectacle mark, 1-2 m, found across India
- **Neurotoxic.** Drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty swallowing and speaking, then paralysis of the breathing muscles
- Local swelling and tissue death at the bite site is common

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 1: The Big Four
children.text:
**2. Common Krait (Bungarus caeruleus / karait)**
- Slim, glossy blue-black with paired white bands, up to 1.7 m
- **The most dangerous snake in India for one reason: the bite is often painless and the person goes to sleep.** Kraits enter houses at night and bite people sleeping on the floor. The victim wakes with abdominal pain, or does not wake at all.
- **Neurotoxic**, with very little local swelling — so the bite is dismissed as an insect bite
- **Any person who wakes at night with unexplained severe abdominal pain, difficulty opening their eyes, or difficulty swallowing, in a krait area, must be taken to hospital immediately as a suspected krait bite.**

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 1: The Big Four
children.text:
**3. Russell's Viper (Daboia russelii)**
- Heavy-bodied, brown with three rows of dark oval spots ringed in black and white, loud hiss
- **Haemotoxic.** Severe pain and swelling, bleeding from gums and injection sites, blood in urine, and **kidney failure**
- The commonest cause of snakebite death in many Indian states

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 1: The Big Four
children.text:
**4. Saw-scaled Viper (Echis carinatus)**
- Small, under 60 cm, rough keeled scales it rubs together to make a sizzling sound
- **Haemotoxic**, causes persistent bleeding and non-clotting blood
- Very common in arid and semi-arid India

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 1: The Big Four
children.text: **Also dangerous but not covered well by standard polyvalent ASV:** the hump-nosed pit viper (Western Ghats, Sri Lanka region) and the king cobra. Hospitals in those regions know this.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 2: Snakebite First Aid — What To Do
children.text:
**The mnemonic is: Do It R.I.G.H.T. — Reassure, Immobilise, Get to Hospital, Tell the doctor.**
1. **Reassure the person.** Around 70% of snakebites in India are by non-venomous snakes, and of venomous bites, many are "dry bites" with no venom injected. Panic raises heart rate and speeds venom spread. Say this out loud to them: "Most snakebites are not fatal. We are going to the hospital now. Stay still."
2. **Immobilise the bitten limb** exactly as you would a fracture — with a splint and a sling. **Do not let them walk if you can avoid it.** Muscle movement pumps venom into the circulation.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 2: Snakebite First Aid — What To Do
children.text:
3. **Keep the bite at or below heart level.**
4. **Remove rings, bangles, chudiyan, watches, anklets, and tight clothing** from the bitten limb immediately, before swelling begins. Swelling traps them and they cut off circulation.
5. **Get to a hospital that stocks ASV. Now.** Not a traditional healer, not a temple, not a local clinic without ASV. Ask specifically: "Do you have anti-snake venom?" District hospitals and most CHCs stock it; PHCs increasingly do.
6. **Note the time of the bite** and write it down.
7. **Photograph the snake from a safe distance if it is already dead or clearly visible.** **Do not try to catch or kill it** — a large share of second bites happen to people trying to capture the snake. Identification is helpful but not required; Indian polyvalent ASV covers all four.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 2: Snakebite First Aid — What To Do
children.text:
8. **Watch the breathing.** In neurotoxic envenoming, the person dies because their breathing muscles stop, not because of the venom itself. If they stop breathing on the way, **rescue breaths or bag-mask ventilation keeps them alive until ASV works.** Many krait and cobra deaths in India are people who could have been ventilated.
9. **Mark the edge of the swelling with a pen every 15 minutes** and note the time. This tells the doctor how fast the envenoming is progressing.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text:
Every one of these is common in India and every one of them causes harm.
- **DO NOT apply a tourniquet.** This is the single most damaging traditional practice. Tourniquets do not stop venom spread; they cause limb ischaemia, gangrene, and amputation, and when released they can dump a bolus of venom into the circulation. **If someone has already applied one, do not remove it until you are at a hospital with ASV available** — sudden release can cause collapse.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT cut the bite site.** It causes uncontrollable bleeding in viper bites and introduces infection.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT suck the venom out** — by mouth, with a syringe, or with a "snake stone". It does not work and it poisons the sucker's mouth ulcers.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT apply ice, chemicals, herbs, cow dung, chillies, kerosene, or a hot iron.**

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT give alcohol, aspirin, or ibuprofen.** Aspirin and ibuprofen worsen bleeding in viper bites. Paracetamol is acceptable for pain.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT wash or scrub the bite site vigorously** — residual venom on the skin can help identification in some hospitals. Wipe gently.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT go to a traditional healer, a temple, or a "snake-stone" practitioner.** This is the leading cause of death by delay in rural India. Every hour lost is measurable mortality.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 3: Snakebite — What NOT To Do
children.text: - **DO NOT wait to see if symptoms develop.** Go immediately. Krait bites in particular have a delay of hours before the person deteriorates suddenly and irreversibly.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 4: Preventing Snakebite
children.text:
Most Indian snakebites happen to people walking barefoot at night, or sleeping on the floor.
- **Wear closed shoes or gumboots when walking outside after dark**, especially in fields, on bunds, and after rain
- **Always carry a torch at night and use it.** Look where you put your feet and your hands.
- **Sleep on a cot, not on the floor.** This single change would prevent a very large share of Indian krait deaths.
- **Use a mosquito net tucked in under the mattress** — it is also an effective snake barrier

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 4: Preventing Snakebite
children.text:
- **Do not put your hands into holes, under rocks, into grain heaps, woodpiles, or thatch** without looking
- **Keep the area around the house clear** of rubbish, rubble, firewood stacks, and dense vegetation — these harbour rats, and rats bring snakes
- **Store grain in sealed containers** and control rodents
- **Close gaps under doors** at night
- **Shake out shoes, clothes, and bedding** before use
- **During floods, expect snakes on any high ground, in houses, and in debris.** Check before you sit, lie down, or reach.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 5: Scorpions and Spiders
children.text:
**Scorpion sting** — the Indian red scorpion (Hottentotta tamulus) of Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka and Andhra is genuinely dangerous, particularly to children.
- **Signs of serious envenoming:** severe local pain, sweating, vomiting, restlessness, cold clammy extremities, and then **pulmonary oedema and heart failure** in children
- **Treatment:** clean the site, cold compress for pain, paracetamol, and **get to a hospital**. Prazosin is the specific treatment for Indian red scorpion envenoming and it is highly effective; scorpion antivenom is also available.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 5: Scorpions and Spiders
children.text:
- Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
**Spiders** — no Indian spider is reliably lethal to a healthy adult. Clean the bite, cold compress, watch for infection and for spreading tissue damage, and see a doctor if it worsens.
**Centipedes** — painful but not dangerous. Wash, cold compress, painkiller.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text: **India accounts for roughly a third of the world's rabies deaths.** Rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms appear and 100% preventable before they do. Dogs cause most cases; monkeys, cats, bats, mongooses, and jackals also transmit it.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text:
**Immediately after any bite, scratch, or lick on broken skin:**
1. **Wash the wound with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes.** This is not a formality — thorough washing alone reduces rabies risk substantially. Use plenty of water and physically flush the wound.
2. **Apply an antiseptic** — povidone-iodine (Betadine) or alcohol — after washing.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text:
3. **Do not apply chilli powder, oil, turmeric, lime, or herbs. Do not suture the wound. Do not cauterise.** These are common Indian practices and all of them increase risk.
4. **Go for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.** The anti-rabies vaccine is **free at government hospitals across India.** Do not delay for any reason.
5. **For a deep bite, a bite on the head, neck, face, hands, or genitals, or multiple bites, you also need rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)** infiltrated into the wound. Ask for it specifically. It is available at district hospitals and medical colleges.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text:
6. **Complete the full vaccine schedule.** Stopping halfway because the dog "looks fine" is a common and fatal error.
7. **Get a tetanus booster** if it has been over 5 years.
8. **Observe the animal if possible** for 10 days — but **start the vaccine anyway**. If the animal is alive and well after 10 days, the course can sometimes be stopped on medical advice.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text:
**Category of exposure:**
- Touching or feeding an animal, licks on intact skin — no PEP needed
- Nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches without bleeding — vaccine
- Single or multiple bites or scratches that break the skin, licks on broken skin, contact with bats — **vaccine plus immunoglobulin**

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text: **Monkey bites** are extremely common in Indian temple towns, hill stations, and cities. Treat exactly as above. Monkeys also transmit herpes B virus.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 6: Dog, Monkey and Animal Bites — Rabies
children.text: **Snake, dog, and monkey bites all need tetanus cover.**

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 7: Insect Stings and Anaphylaxis
children.text:
**Bee, wasp and hornet stings:**
- **Remove a bee sting by scraping sideways** with a card or a fingernail. Do not squeeze it with tweezers — that injects the remaining venom.
- Wash, apply a cold compress, take an antihistamine (cetirizine) for itching
- **Multiple stings (dozens to hundreds) can cause kidney failure and are a medical emergency**, even without allergy. Indian giant honeybee (Apis dorsata) mass attacks are a real hazard near forests and old buildings.
- **If attacked by a swarm: run, in a straight line, covering your face, for at least 100 metres.** Do not swat, do not jump into water (they wait), do not stand still. Get indoors or into a vehicle.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 7: Insect Stings and Anaphylaxis
children.text:
**Anaphylaxis** — the emergency. Signs within minutes: swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat; a tight throat or hoarse voice; wheeze or difficulty breathing; widespread rash; dizziness or collapse.
- **Adrenaline into the outer thigh is the treatment** if an auto-injector is available. Through clothing is fine.
- **Lie them flat with the legs raised** unless they cannot breathe lying down, in which case sit them up. **Do not let them stand or walk** — this can cause sudden fatal collapse.
- **An antihistamine tablet is not treatment for anaphylaxis.** Get to a hospital urgently.
- Anyone who has had one severe reaction should carry an adrenaline auto-injector.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 8: Leeches, Ticks and Water Hazards
children.text:
**Leeches** (Western Ghats, North East, monsoon forests): do not pull, burn, or apply salt while attached — this makes them regurgitate into the wound. Slide a fingernail or a card sideways under the sucker to detach. Then clean and press — leech bites bleed for hours because of the anticoagulant, which is harmless. Cover with a dressing. Prevent with tucked-in trousers, leech socks, and tobacco or salt paste on footwear.
**Ticks:** grasp as close to the skin as possible with tweezers and pull straight out, steadily. Do not twist, burn, or smother with oil. Clean the site. Watch for fever and rash over the next 2 weeks — India has scrub typhus, Indian tick typhus, and Kyasanur Forest Disease (Western Ghats), all of which are treatable and dangerous if missed.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 8: Leeches, Ticks and Water Hazards
children.text:
**Mosquitoes:** the biggest killer insect in India. Malaria, dengue, chikungunya, and Japanese encephalitis all follow floods and standing water. Use nets, cover up at dawn and dusk (dengue mosquitoes bite by day), use repellent, and **eliminate all standing water** — coolers, pots, tyres, tanks, and roof gutters — every week.
**Stonefish, sea urchins and stingrays** (Indian coasts): for stonefish and stingray, **immerse the wound in water as hot as can be tolerated for 30-90 minutes** — the venom is heat-labile and this genuinely relieves pain. Remove visible spines. Get medical care; these wounds infect badly and stingray barbs can penetrate deeply.

children.heading_path: Snakebite, Animal Bites and Stings (India) > Part 8: Leeches, Ticks and Water Hazards
children.text: **Jellyfish** (common on Indian coasts, especially the west coast in monsoon): rinse with **seawater or vinegar, not fresh water** — fresh water triggers remaining stinging cells to fire. Remove tentacles with a card or gloved hand, not bare fingers. Then hot water immersion for pain. Do not urinate on it.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India)
children.text: After the first 24 hours of any Indian disaster, the threat shifts from the event itself to what follows: contaminated water, spoiled food, and failed sanitation. **Diarrhoeal disease has killed more people in Indian disasters than the disasters themselves.**

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 1: How Much Water You Actually Need
children.text:
- **3 litres per person per day is the survival minimum** for drinking alone, in normal Indian conditions.
- **In summer heat (above 40 C), or with physical work, this doubles to 6 litres or more.**
- Add roughly 2-3 litres per person per day for cooking and basic hygiene.
- **Children, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and the elderly need proportionally more and dehydrate faster.**

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 1: How Much Water You Actually Need
children.text: - **Do not ration drinking water below your need in order to make it last.** Dehydration impairs judgement within hours and that kills you faster than running out. Ration your activity and your exposure to heat instead — find shade, stay still, work at night.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 1: How Much Water You Actually Need
children.text: **Signs you are dehydrated:** dark yellow urine; passing urine less than 3-4 times a day; dry mouth; headache; dizziness on standing; tiredness; irritability. In infants: fewer than 6 wet nappies a day, no tears when crying, sunken eyes, a sunken soft spot on the head, and lethargy.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 2: Where to Find Water in an Indian Emergency
children.text:
**Inside a building, in order of safety:**
1. **The overhead tank (Sintex/RCC tank on the roof)** — most Indian buildings hold 500-1000 litres up there. Usually still clean. This is your primary emergency reserve.
2. **The underground sump** — larger but more likely to be contaminated. Treat it.
3. **The geyser/water heater tank** — 10-25 litres of clean water. Switch off the power, let it cool, and drain from the bottom outlet.
4. **The toilet cistern** (the tank above, not the bowl) — clean if no chemical block is used.
5. **Ice in the freezer**, melted
6. **The water in pipes** — open the highest tap in the building to let air in, then drain from the lowest tap

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 2: Where to Find Water in an Indian Emergency
children.text:
7. **Water in a cooler, RO reject water (treat it), canned vegetables and dal liquid, coconut water**
**Outside:**
- **Rainwater** — the cleanest natural source in India. Catch it in the open with a clean sheet, tarpaulin, or vessel. **Discard the first few minutes of runoff from a roof** (it carries dust, bird droppings, and roof debris), then collect. Still worth treating.
- **Handpumps and borewells** — generally safer than surface water because the source is deep, but they get contaminated in floods when the water table rises over the wellhead. Treat anyway.
- **Rivers, tanks, ponds, and canals** — always treat. Take from a flowing part, upstream of habitation, away from banks.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 2: Where to Find Water in an Indian Emergency
children.text:
- **Dew** — wipe grass or leaves with a cloth at dawn and wring it out. Surprisingly productive.
- **Transpiration bag** — tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch of a non-poisonous tree in the sun. Water condenses over several hours.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 2: Where to Find Water in an Indian Emergency
children.text: - **Do not drink:** seawater, urine, floodwater, standing water in a collapse void, water from a well that tastes salty, water near a factory outfall, or any water with an oily sheen or an unnatural colour or smell.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text: **Always filter before you treat.** Pour through several folded layers of clean cotton cloth — a folded saree is a genuinely effective pre-filter and removes sediment, larvae, and copepods. Sediment protects pathogens from chlorine and blocks UV.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text:
**Method 1 — Boiling (most reliable).**
- Bring to a **rolling boil for 1 minute** (3 minutes above 2,000 m — Himachal, Uttarakhand, Ladakh, Sikkim).
- Kills all bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Does not remove chemicals, salt, or heavy metals.
- Let it cool covered. Pour between two vessels to restore taste.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text:
**Method 2 — Chlorine tablets.**
- Aquatabs, halazone, or the tablets distributed by health departments. Follow the packet — typically 1 tablet per litre, wait 30 minutes.
- Does not kill Cryptosporidium. Combine with filtration.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text:
**Method 3 — Household bleach (sodium hypochlorite).**
- Use **plain, unscented** bleach only — no detergent, no fragrance, no colour-safe additives.
- Roughly **2 drops per litre of clear water, 4 drops per litre of cloudy water**. Stir and wait 30 minutes.
- **It should smell faintly of chlorine afterwards.** If not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text:
**Method 4 — SODIS (solar disinfection).** Excellent in Indian sunlight and costs nothing.
- Fill a **clear** PET bottle (not more than 2-3 litres, not glass, not coloured) with **clear** water, no more than 10 cm deep when lying down.
- Lay it horizontally on a **dark or metal surface** — a tin roof is ideal — in full sun.
- **6 hours of strong sun, or 2 consecutive days if cloudy.**
- Does not work on cloudy water. Filter first.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text:
**Method 5 — Ceramic candle filters, RO, and household purifiers.**
- Most Indian homes have one. **Candle filters and RO membranes remove bacteria and protozoa but many do not remove viruses,** and RO needs electricity and pressure.
- **Boil filtered water too** during an outbreak.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 3: Making Water Safe
children.text: **What treatment does NOT fix:** salinity, pesticide, heavy metals (fluoride, arsenic — endemic in parts of West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Punjab, and Rajasthan), and industrial chemicals. Boiling actually **concentrates** these. If the water is chemically contaminated, find another source.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 4: Storing Water
children.text:
- **Store in clean, food-grade containers with lids.** Used cooking-oil tins and jerry cans, well washed, are fine. Do not use containers that held chemicals or pesticide.
- **Keep treated and untreated water clearly separated**, and mark them.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 4: Storing Water
children.text:
- **Never dip hands or a cup into a storage container.** Pour, or use a dedicated ladle with a long handle. Hands are the main route of recontamination in a relief setting.
- **Store in the dark and the cool.** Sunlight grows algae.
- **Re-treat stored water every 2-3 days** in Indian heat, or boil before drinking.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text:
**Priority order for eating what you have:**
1. Perishables from the fridge, in the first 4-6 hours after power fails
2. Freezer contents next — a full freezer stays cold for about 48 hours if unopened, half full for about 24
3. Cupboard staples and dry goods
4. Sealed packets and cans last

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text:
**Throw away without tasting:**
- Anything that touched floodwater, **including sealed packets** (seals are not waterproof) and anything with a screw cap or a crimped top
- Cooked food left at Indian room temperature for more than 2 hours
- Anything with mould, a bad smell, a slimy texture, or an off colour
- Cans that are swollen, leaking, badly dented at the seam, or rusted through
- Any milk, curd, paneer, or meat that has been unrefrigerated

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text: **Cans that are intact** can be salvaged from floodwater: remove the label, wash in soapy water, disinfect in a chlorine solution, dry, and relabel with a marker.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text:
**Good emergency foods for an Indian household — no cooking, long shelf life, high energy:**
- Roasted chana, sattu, murmura, chuda/poha, dry fruit, peanuts
- Gur (jaggery), glucose powder, honey
- Biscuits, rusk, khakhra, thepla (lasts several days)
- Ready-to-eat packets, canned dal and vegetables
- **ORS sachets — the highest-value item per gram in any Indian emergency kit**
- Milk powder, and for infants, formula if already in use

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text: **Rationing:** eat less but eat something every day. **Do not eat if you have no water** — digestion consumes water and dry food worsens dehydration. Water first, always.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 5: Food
children.text:
**Cooking without gas:**
- A three-stone fire, a chulha, or a rocket stove made from a tin can
- **Never cook with charcoal, coal, or a kerosene stove inside a closed room.** Carbon monoxide is invisible, odourless, and kills whole families in their sleep. Ventilate on two sides at minimum.
- A solar cooker or a black pot in strong sun will pasteurise water and cook dal slowly

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 6: Sanitation — This Is What Kills
children.text:
The single most important thing you can do to prevent an outbreak is to keep faeces away from water, food, and hands.
**Setting up a latrine when there is none:**
- **At least 30 metres from any water source, and downhill from it.** This is the number that matters.
- A **trench latrine**: dig a trench 30 cm wide, 60-90 cm deep, as long as needed. Keep the excavated soil beside it and **cover each use with soil or ash**.
- **Cat-hole** for one person: 20 cm deep, covered after each use, at least 30 m from water.
- **Bucket toilet with a lid** for a house or a shelter: line it, add ash or lime after each use, and empty into a deep pit far from water and habitation.
- **Mark the latrine area clearly** and keep it away from the cooking and sleeping area.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 6: Sanitation — This Is What Kills
children.text: - **Provide a handwashing point at the exit** — even a bottle with a hole in the cap hanging from a string, and a bar of soap on a string.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 6: Sanitation — This Is What Kills
children.text:
**Handwashing is the single highest-impact intervention in a relief setting.**
- With soap, for 20 seconds, before eating, before cooking, after the toilet, after handling waste, after handling a body, after touching a sick person
- **A "tippy tap"** — a hanging bottle or can with a small hole, tipped by a foot lever — uses a fraction of the water of a tap and works in a camp
- If you have no soap: ash and sand rubbed on wet hands is genuinely effective. Plain water is much better than nothing.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 6: Sanitation — This Is What Kills
children.text: **Menstrual hygiene** is routinely neglected in Indian relief settings and causes real harm. Ensure a private space, water, soap, cloth or pads, and a disposal point. Cloth must be washed in clean water, dried in **direct sunlight** (not hidden in the dark, which causes infection), and stored dry.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 6: Sanitation — This Is What Kills
children.text:
**Waste and bodies:**
- Bury or burn organic waste. Keep it away from the water source and downwind.
- **Dead bodies do not cause epidemics** — this is a persistent and harmful myth that has led to mass burials without identification in Indian disasters. Handle them with dignity, use gloves, wash hands, **photograph and record identifying details before burial**, and follow the district administration's instructions. The living, not the dead, are the source of disease.
- **Dead animals** are a genuine hazard and should be buried deep, away from water, or disposed of as directed.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text: **ORS is the treatment. Fluid, not medicine, is what saves lives.**

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text:
**Making ORS correctly:**
- **One full WHO-formula sachet in exactly 1 litre of clean water.** Not more concentrated — a stronger solution is dangerous, especially for children.
- **Homemade if you have no sachet:** **6 level teaspoons of sugar + half a level teaspoon of salt in 1 litre of clean water.** Stir until dissolved.
- **Taste it. It should be no saltier than tears.** If it is saltier, throw it away and remake it.
- Discard after 24 hours and make fresh.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text:
**Giving it:**
- **Small sips, continuously.** A spoonful every 1-2 minutes for a child.
- **Keep giving it even if they are vomiting.** Wait 10 minutes after a vomit and restart with smaller, slower sips. Some gets absorbed.
- **After every loose stool:** a child under 2 needs about a quarter to half a cup; an older child about half to one cup; an adult as much as they will take.
- **Keep breastfeeding an infant.** Do not stop. Breast milk is the best fluid an infant can have.
- **Keep feeding.** Withholding food prolongs diarrhoea and causes malnutrition. Give khichdi, curd, banana, rice water (kanji), dal water.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text: - **Zinc supplements for 14 days** shorten childhood diarrhoea significantly and are available free at government facilities.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text:
**Danger signs — get to a hospital:**
- Blood in the stool
- Repeated vomiting so nothing stays down
- No urine for 8 hours (adult) or 6 hours (child)
- Sunken eyes, skin that stays tented when pinched, a sunken fontanelle in an infant
- Lethargy, floppiness, or difficulty waking
- Sunken eyes with cold, mottled hands and feet
- High fever
- **Rice-water stools in huge volume with rapid collapse — this is cholera and it needs IV fluids and antibiotics urgently**

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 7: Diarrhoea and ORS
children.text: **Do not give anti-diarrhoeal drugs (loperamide) to children.** They trap the infection and cause serious harm.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 8: Disease to Expect After an Indian Disaster
children.text:
| Disease | Onset | Key sign | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acute watery diarrhoea / cholera | 1-5 days | Rice-water stool, rapid dehydration | ORS immediately, hospital for severe |
| Typhoid | 1-3 weeks | Stepwise rising fever, abdominal pain | Doctor, antibiotics |
| Hepatitis A and E | 2-8 weeks | Jaundice, dark urine, nausea. **Hepatitis E is very dangerous in pregnancy** | Rest, fluids, doctor |
| Leptospirosis | 2-30 days | Fever, severe calf pain, red eyes, jaundice, after wading in floodwater | **Doctor urgently — treatable, lethal if missed** |
| Dengue | 4-10 days | High fever, severe body ache, rash, low platelets | Fluids, paracetamol only. **No aspirin or ibuprofen.** Watch for warning signs |
| Malaria | 1-4 weeks | Fever with chills, often cyclical | Test and treat |
| Scrub typhus | 1-3 weeks | Fever, an eschar (black scab) at a bite site | Doctor — doxycycline works |
| Measles | 1-2 weeks | Fever, rash, in crowded camps | Vaccinate children in camps |
| Skin and fungal infection | Days | Rashes, itching between toes | Keep dry, antifungal |
| Respiratory infection | Days | Cough, fever, in crowded shelters | Ventilate, separate the sick |

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 8: Disease to Expect After an Indian Disaster
children.text: **Dengue warning signs that mean go to hospital now:** severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from gums or nose, black stools, restlessness or lethargy, cold clammy skin, and a sudden drop in temperature with worsening condition.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 9: Camp and Shelter Hygiene
children.text:
- **Ventilate.** Respiratory infection and TB spread fast in crowded, closed shelters.
- **Separate the sick**, especially anyone with diarrhoea or a cough, and give them a dedicated toilet or bucket if possible.
- **One food handler, with clean hands, serving everyone** is safer than everyone serving themselves.
- **Cook thoroughly and eat immediately.** Do not store cooked food in Indian heat.
- **Cover all food and water.** Flies are the main vector.
- **Empty all standing water weekly** — coolers, pots, tyres, tarpaulin folds — to stop mosquito breeding.
- **Vaccinate children** — measles and the routine schedule — as soon as health teams arrive. Camps are where outbreaks start.

children.heading_path: Water, Food and Sanitation in a Cutoff (India) > Part 9: Camp and Shelter Hygiene
children.text: - **Report clusters of illness immediately** to the health worker, ANM, or ASHA. Early reporting is what stops an outbreak.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India)
children.text:
This guide covers keeping a body at a survivable temperature and finding your way when you are cut off — whether that is in a collapsed town, on a stranded highway, in a forest, in the Thar, or on a Himalayan road blocked by a slide.
**Shelter is the second priority after airway and bleeding, ahead of water and far ahead of food.** In Indian conditions, "shelter" usually means shade and airflow, not a roof against snow. Get that ranking right and it changes what you build.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 1: What Shelter Is Actually For
children.text:
Ask: **what is trying to kill me?**
- **Sun and heat (most of India, most of the year):** you need **shade and moving air**, and nothing else. A tarpaulin stretched a foot above your head with open sides is vastly better than an enclosed tent, which becomes an oven.
- **Cold and wind (Himalaya, north Indian winter nights, high altitude):** you need **insulation, a windbreak, and separation from the ground**. Ground conduction steals more heat than air ever will.
- **Rain (monsoon India):** you need a **waterproof roof and to stay dry**. Wet clothing at 15 C causes hypothermia. Wetness kills more than cold does.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 1: What Shelter Is Actually For
children.text:
- **Insects (everywhere, especially post-flood):** you need a **net or a smoke source**. Malaria and dengue are the delayed killers.
- **People:** you need to be **out of sight** or behind a locked door.
Build for the actual threat. Do not build a cave in Rajasthan or an open lean-to in Spiti.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 2: Site Selection
children.text:
Get this right and the shelter itself hardly matters.
**Avoid:**
- **Dry riverbeds, nalas, gullies, and the bottom of any drainage line.** Flash floods. This is the most common fatal camping error in India.
- **The base of a cliff or a cut slope** — rockfall and landslide
- **Under a lone tall tree** — lightning, and in India, falling branches from silk cotton, eucalyptus, and old peepal
- **Under coconut palms** — a falling coconut is lethal
- **Hilltops and open ridges** — wind and lightning
- **Low hollows in cold areas** — cold air pools there at night
- **Directly beside standing water** — mosquitoes
- **Anthills, termite mounds, and rat burrows** — snakes hunt there

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 2: Site Selection
children.text:
**Prefer:**
- **Slightly raised, level, dry ground** with natural drainage
- **On the leeward side of a wall, rock, or dense vegetation** for a windbreak
- **Near but not beside water** — 50-100 m
- **Where you can be seen from the air or a road** if you want rescue
- **Where there is fuel and building material**

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 3: Shelter in a Damaged Town or City
children.text:
- **Do not sleep inside a structurally damaged building.** See the **Earthquake** guide for how to read damage.
- **A vehicle** is a workable shelter: rain-proof, lockable, and elevated. In heat, it is lethal in daytime and fine at night — park in shade, keep windows cracked, never sleep in a running vehicle (carbon monoxide).
- **Under a stairwell, in a doorway of a sound building, or in the lee of a compound wall**
- **A tarpaulin lean-to** against a sound wall: tie two corners high, stake two corners low, and you have a rain and sun shelter in 3 minutes.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 3: Shelter in a Damaged Town or City
children.text:
- **Schools, temples, mosques, gurudwaras, churches, community halls, and panchayat bhavans** are the standard relief shelters in India and are usually the first to open. Go there rather than improvising.
- **Insulate from concrete.** A concrete floor pulls heat out of you all night. Cardboard, plastic sheet, dry leaves, newspaper, a durrie — anything between you and the slab is worth more than an extra blanket on top.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Tarpaulin / plastic sheet A-frame (5 minutes)**
Run a rope between two anchors at chest height. Drape the sheet over it. Weight the edges with stones. Done. Add a second sheet on the ground.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Lean-to (rain and wind from one direction)**
One horizontal pole between two supports at waist-to-chest height, angled poles or branches leaning from it to the ground on the windward side, covered with leaves, thatch, or a sheet, layered from the bottom up like roof tiles so water runs off.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Debris hut (cold weather, one person, no tools)**
A ridge pole from a low fork to the ground. Ribs leaning against it on both sides. Pile 60 cm or more of leaves, grass, and debris over the whole thing. Stuff the inside with dry leaves and crawl in. **The thickness of the debris is the insulation** — this shelter works down to freezing with no fire.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Shade shelter (Indian summer — the one you will most often need)**
The critical detail: **two layers with an air gap between them.** A sheet stretched flat, and a second sheet 20-30 cm above it. The air gap carries away the radiant heat and the temperature underneath drops by 10-15 C compared to a single layer. Keep all sides open for airflow. Orient the long axis east-west so the sun tracks along it.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Desert shelter (Thar, Kutch)**
Dig a shallow trench 30-45 cm deep — the sand a few inches down is dramatically cooler. Cover with a sheet raised above it. Rest during the day, move at night.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 4: Improvised Shelters
children.text:
**Snow / high altitude**
A trench in the snow with a covered roof, or a hollow dug into a drift. Insulate the floor thickly. **Keep a ventilation hole** and keep it clear — carbon dioxide accumulates in a sealed snow shelter.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 5: Staying Warm
children.text:
**Layer, and keep the layers dry.**
- **Inner layer:** should wick, not hold water. **Wet cotton against the skin is the single biggest cold-weather mistake in India** — it holds water and conducts heat away. If it is wet, take it off.
- **Middle layer:** traps air. Wool, fleece, a shawl, a blanket, crumpled newspaper stuffed between layers.
- **Outer layer:** blocks wind and water. A plastic sheet, a raincoat, a tarpaulin poncho.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 5: Staying Warm
children.text:
**Get off the ground.** A layer of dry leaves, cardboard, plastic, or a durrie underneath is worth more than two blankets on top.
**Cover the head, neck, hands and feet.** A monkey cap, a muffler, a towel — anything.
**Newspaper is excellent insulation.** Stuff it inside clothing, under a shirt, inside shoes, and between blankets.
**Share body heat.** Two or three people under one set of blankets, with insulation underneath, stay far warmer than three people separately.
**Eat and drink warm things.** The body needs fuel to generate heat. A hot sweet tea genuinely helps.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 5: Staying Warm
children.text: **Never bring a coal angithi, sigri, charcoal, or a kerosene heater into a closed room to sleep.** Carbon monoxide kills whole families every north Indian winter. If you use one, ventilate on two sides and put it out before sleeping.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 6: Fire
children.text: **Uses:** warmth, boiling water (the most important use), cooking, light, keeping animals and insects away, signalling, and morale.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 6: Fire
children.text:
**Building it:**
1. **Tinder** — anything that catches from a spark: dry grass, coconut coir, cotton wool, jute, a bird's nest, dry bark shavings, paper, char cloth. **Coconut coir and dry cow dung are the classic Indian tinders** and both work well.
2. **Kindling** — pencil-thick dry twigs, split bamboo
3. **Fuel** — progressively thicker dead wood, dry dung cakes (uple), bamboo
4. Build a small teepee of kindling over the tinder, light from the upwind side, and add fuel gradually. **Do not smother a young flame.**

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 6: Fire
children.text:
**Ignition without matches:**
- **A lighter or matches, kept in a sealed plastic bag** — prepare this, do not rely on improvisation
- **A vehicle battery**: brush the two terminals with a wire or steel wool to spark into tinder
- **A magnifying lens, a spectacle lens, a camera lens, or the bottom of a clear bottle filled with water** focused on tinder in strong Indian sun — this works well and is the most practical improvised method here
- **A ferrocerium rod** — put one in your kit
- **Friction (bow drill)** — works, takes practice, and takes an hour if you have never done it. Do not rely on it.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 6: Fire
children.text:
**Safety:** clear a metre of bare ground around the fire, never leave it unattended, never build under a low canopy or against a dry thatch wall, keep water or sand ready, and **never build a fire inside a closed shelter or a tent**.
**Cooking and boiling:** a steel tiffin box, a bottle cut in half, or even a plastic bottle held just above the flame with water in it (the water stops it melting) will boil water.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 7: If You Are Stranded
children.text:
**On a highway or in a vehicle:**
- **Stay with the vehicle.** It is shelter, it is visible, and it is what searchers look for. People who walk away from vehicles in the Thar, in Ladakh, and on blocked Himalayan roads are the ones who die.
- Run the engine and heater for 10 minutes an hour in cold, **with the exhaust pipe kept clear of snow or mud** and a window slightly open. Carbon monoxide from a blocked exhaust kills.
- In heat, **get out of the vehicle and shelter in its shade**, not inside it. Use the bonnet or a sheet stretched from the doors.
- Tie something bright to the antenna or the door handle. Raise the bonnet — the universal Indian signal for a broken-down vehicle.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 7: If You Are Stranded
children.text:
- Ration water; do not ration your decision to seek shade.
**On foot and lost:**
- **STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan.** Sit down for five minutes before doing anything. Most people who die lost, died from moving badly, not from being lost.
- **Stay put if anyone knows where you were going.** Rescue finds stationary people.
- **If you must move: follow water downhill.** In India, watercourses lead to villages. But **do not enter a gorge you cannot climb out of**, and do not follow a river in the Himalaya through a cliff section.
- **Follow power lines, a pipeline, a fence line, or a canal** — all lead to habitation.

children.heading_path: Shelter, Warmth and Being Stranded (India) > Part 7: If You Are Stranded
children.text:
- **Move in the cool** — early morning and evening in the plains, midday in the mountains in winter.
